title: Section 2
context: A coordinator is giving an induction talk to new volunteers at a maritime museum.

audio.t: You will hear a museum coordinator giving a talk to new volunteers at the Harbourside Maritime Museum.
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Harbourside Maritime Museum. I'm Karen, and I coordinate our volunteer team.
First, let me explain how much time we ask from you. We used to ask for one shift every week, but that was too much for many people.
So now the minimum is two shifts a month, and each shift lasts four hours. Most of you will find that easy to fit around work or study.
Before your first shift, you'll need your volunteer badge. You'd normally collect it from the main reception, but there is building work there this month.
I thought we'd moved it to the security office, but sorry, I was wrong. You'll find your badge in the volunteer office on the first floor, next to the library.
Safety comes first here. If a visitor feels unwell, please don't try to treat them yourself.
Stay with the person and use your radio to call one of our first-aiders. The security desk deals with lost property and building problems, not medical issues.
Now, what do you get in return? Everyone receives a discount in our gift shop from the very first day.
Once you've completed fifty hours, you'll receive free annual membership of the museum. And at one hundred hours, you also get a certificate.
Our next training session is on Tuesday. I originally planned to cover first aid, but the trainer is unavailable, so we'll postpone that until next month.
Instead, Tuesday's session will teach you how to help visitors with accessibility needs, such as wheelchair users or people with hearing difficulties.
Now let me take you through the museum and tell you what you'll be doing in each area. We'll start with the Navigation Gallery on the ground floor.
This gallery is full of old compasses, maps and sextants. Volunteers here show visitors how those instruments were used at sea.
Next door is the Children's Discovery Room, which is always busy at weekends. Your job there is to help families with the craft activities, like making paper boats.

Upstairs we have the Temporary Exhibition space, which is currently showing historic paintings of the harbour. It's a quiet area, and you only need to remind visitors that flash photography isn't allowed.
Next to it is the Archive Room. It holds thousands of donated photographs, and volunteers there sort them and write labels so they can be catalogued.
Please remember that the photographs are delicate, so you must wear gloves at all times in that room.
The last area is the Shipbuilding Hall, where we're restoring a wooden fishing boat. Volunteers here wear a hard hat and lead short tours explaining how the boat is being repaired.
You may also have noticed the Café Terrace. We employ our own staff there, so volunteers aren't needed, but you're welcome to use it during your breaks.
Right, does anyone have any questions before we start our walk round the museum?
